senses.definition: before now, by the length of time stated
senses.explanation: Ago comes after the length of time (two days ago, a long time ago) and measures back from the present moment. It goes with the simple past, not the present perfect: We moved here three years ago. To measure back from a time in the past, use before or earlier: I had met her two years before.

examples.text: Kim moved here three years ago.
I saw Omar a few minutes ago.
It all happened a long time ago, before you were born.
How long ago did you order?
examples.note: how long ago: asking how far back

compare.note: before or earlier counts back from a time in the past, not from now: I had met her two years before
since gives the starting point; ago gives the distance back: since Monday, three days ago
for gives the length of a period: for three days

usage_note: Ago is never used on its own or before the time phrase: two days ago, not ago two days. A long time ago and long ago mean the same; long ago is more literary.

learner_errors.incorrect: I came here before two days.
learner_errors.correct: I came here two days ago.
learner_errors.note: Ago, not before, counts back from now, and it comes after the time phrase.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have lived here since three years ago.
learner_errors.correct: I have lived here for three years.
learner_errors.note: Since takes a starting point (since Monday) and for takes a length (for three years); ago is not used after since.

learner_errors.incorrect: I have seen him two days ago.
learner_errors.correct: I saw him two days ago.
learner_errors.note: Ago fixes a finished time in the past, so the verb is the simple past, not the present perfect.

etymology.text: Ago is a short form of agone, the past participle of an old verb meaning to go by or pass away. Two days ago was two days gone, which is why ago comes after the time phrase, like a participle.

adaptation.semantic: Ago measures back from the moment of speaking. Counting back from a time in the past uses before or earlier: I had seen him two days before.
adaptation.grammar: Ago follows the time phrase and points back from now; it takes the simple past, not the present perfect: she left two hours ago. Many languages put the equivalent word before the time phrase or use a preposition; the English order is fixed.
adaptation.pronunciation: Two syllables with the stress on the second; the first is the weak ə, as in about.
